meaning: Stop doing something that you have done regularly for a long time.
japanese: 習慣をやめる。癖を断つ。
cue: You keep checking your phone in bed and cannot stop.
reply: It's hard to break a habit you've had for years.
replyJapanese: 何年も続けてきた習慣をやめるのは難しいです。
transferCue: Share good news about a friend who used to bite her nails.
transferReply: She finally broke the habit of biting her nails.
transferReplyJapanese: 彼女はついに、爪をかむ癖をやめました。
frame: Break a habit / break the habit of doing something
nuance: Usually about a bad habit. With of, use the and an -ing form: break the habit of smoking. Kick a habit is more informal.
nuanceJapanese: たいてい悪い習慣について使う。of を続けるときは the と -ing 形にする: break the habit of smoking。kick a habit はよりくだけた言い方。

meaning: Do something better or faster than anyone has done it before.
japanese: 記録を破る。記録を更新する。
cue: Share good news about last month's results.
reply: Our team broke a record for monthly sales in March.
replyJapanese: 私たちのチームは、3月に月間売上の記録を更新しました。
transferCue: Describe the end of a swimming race.
transferReply: She broke the record by half a second in the final.
transferReplyJapanese: 彼女は決勝で、記録を0.5秒更新しました。
frame: Break a record / the record for something
nuance: Use the for one known record: break the world record. Beat a record means the same; set a record means make a new one.
nuanceJapanese: 特定の記録には the を使う: break the world record。beat a record も同じ意味。set a record は新記録を作ること。

meaning: Do something that the law does not allow.
japanese: 法律を破る。法律に違反する。
cue: Someone asks if it is fine to cycle on the pavement.
reply: You're breaking the law if you cycle on the pavement here.
replyJapanese: ここで歩道を自転車で走ると、法律違反になりますよ。
transferCue: Give a fair view of a company that people are angry with.
transferReply: The company was unfair, but it didn't break the law.
transferReplyJapanese: その会社のやり方は不公平でしたが、法律は破っていません。
nuance: Usually the law, meaning the whole legal system; break a law points to one particular rule. Obey the law is the opposite.
nuanceJapanese: ふつう the law で法制度全体を指す。break a law は特定の法律ひとつを指す。反対は obey the law。

meaning: Make someone feel very sad.
japanese: ひどく悲しませる。胸が張り裂ける思いをさせる。
cue: Your family home has been sold and nobody lives there now.
reply: It breaks my heart to see the old house empty.
replyJapanese: あの古い家が空き家になっているのを見ると、胸が痛みます。
transferCue: Explain how a friend's daughter felt about the school team.
transferReply: It broke her heart when she didn't make the team.
transferReplyJapanese: チームに選ばれなかったとき、彼女はひどく悲しみました。
frame: It breaks your heart to do something
nuance: Your changes with the person: break my heart, break her heart. It is used for a lost love and for any deep sadness. The adjective is heartbroken.
nuanceJapanese: your は人に合わせて変える: break my heart, break her heart。失恋にも、深い悲しみ全般にも使う。形容詞は heartbroken。

meaning: Used to make a question or request sound more polite.
japanese: もしかして。ひょっとして。
cue: You left your umbrella in a café and phone them.
reply: Did anyone hand in a black umbrella by any chance?
replyJapanese: もしかして、黒い傘が届いていませんか。
transferCue: Your phone is nearly dead before a long meeting.
transferReply: Do you have a spare phone charger by any chance?
transferReplyJapanese: ひょっとして、予備の充電器を持っていませんか。
frame: Do you have … by any chance?
nuance: Used only in questions, usually at the end. It suggests that you do not expect a yes, which makes the request softer.
nuanceJapanese: 疑問文だけで使い、ふつう文末に置く。「はい」を期待していない含みがあり、頼みごとがやわらかくなる。

meaning: Without being planned.
japanese: 偶然に。たまたま。
cue: Explain how you saw an old classmate again.
reply: We met by chance at the airport in Lisbon.
replyJapanese: リスボンの空港で、偶然会ったんです。
transferCue: Explain how you found the place where you live.
transferReply: I found this flat by chance while walking the dog.
transferReplyJapanese: 犬の散歩中に、たまたまこの部屋を見つけました。
frame: Meet someone / find something by chance
nuance: No article: by chance, not by a chance. By accident is close but often suggests a mistake. On purpose is the opposite.
nuanceJapanese: 冠詞なしで by chance。by a chance とは言わない。by accident は近いが、失敗の含みが出やすい。反対は on purpose。

meaning: Because the law says so.
japanese: 法律で。法律により。
cue: A new colleague wants to throw away old paperwork.
reply: By law, we have to keep these records for seven years.
replyJapanese: 法律で、これらの記録は7年間保管しなければなりません。
transferCue: Tell a visitor about a rule for families who drive.
transferReply: Children under twelve are required by law to use a car seat.
transferReplyJapanese: 12歳未満の子どもは、法律でチャイルドシートの使用が義務づけられています。
frame: By law, … / be required by law to do something
nuance: No article: by law, not by the law. It often goes with must, have to or be required. Against the law means illegal.
nuanceJapanese: 冠詞なしで by law。by the law とは言わない。must, have to, be required とよく一緒に使う。against the law は「違法で」の意味。

meaning: Used to say that something has probably happened or should have happened already.
japanese: 今ごろはもう。もうすでに。
cue: Your friends left for the airport three hours ago.
reply: They should be at the airport by now.
replyJapanese: 今ごろはもう、空港に着いているはずです。
transferCue: Start talking about something the whole office is discussing.
transferReply: You've probably heard the news about the merger by now.
transferReplyJapanese: 合併の知らせは、もう聞いているでしょう。
frame: Should have done something by now
nuance: Often with should, must or probably. Until now is different: it describes a situation that has continued up to this moment.
nuanceJapanese: should, must, probably とよく一緒に使う。until now は別の表現で、今まで続いてきた状況を表す。

meaning: Start to burn.
japanese: 火がつく。燃え出す。
cue: Someone is cooking with a towel next to the gas ring.
reply: Move that towel or it will catch fire.
replyJapanese: そのタオルをどけないと、火がつきますよ。
transferCue: Explain why the traffic was so bad today.
transferReply: A van caught fire on the motorway this morning.
transferReplyJapanese: 今朝、高速道路でバンから火が出ました。
nuance: No article and no object: the thing that burns is the subject. To make something burn, say set fire to it. American English also says catch on fire.
nuanceJapanese: 冠詞も目的語も付かず、燃えるものが主語になる。火をつける側は set fire to を使う。アメリカ英語では catch on fire とも言う。

meaning: See someone or something suddenly or only for a moment.
japanese: ちらりと見かける。ふと目にする。
cue: You noticed a friend at a busy festival.
reply: I caught sight of Mia in the crowd and waved.
replyJapanese: 人混みの中にミアを見かけて、手を振りました。
transferCue: Describe a moment on a train journey along the coast.
transferReply: We caught sight of the sea just before the tunnel.
transferReplyJapanese: トンネルの直前に、海がちらりと見えました。
nuance: No article before sight. It describes one short moment, so it is not used in continuous tenses. Lose sight of is the opposite.
nuanceJapanese: sight に冠詞は付かない。一瞬の出来事なので進行形にはしない。反対は lose sight of。

meaning: Make a lot of progress and become much more successful.
japanese: 大きく進歩する。ずいぶん成長する。
cue: Praise a colleague who used to be nervous in front of people.
reply: You've come a long way since your first presentation.
replyJapanese: 最初のプレゼンの頃から、ずいぶん成長しましたね。
transferCue: Compare today's electric cars with the early ones.
transferReply: Electric cars have come a long way in ten years.
transferReplyJapanese: 電気自動車は、この10年で大きく進歩しました。
nuance: Almost always in the present perfect: have come a long way. Have a long way to go means the opposite, that much progress is still needed.
nuanceJapanese: ほぼ現在完了形 have come a long way で使う。have a long way to go は逆に「まだ先は長い」の意味。

meaning: Appear for a short time and then disappear again.
japanese: 現れては消える。出たり引いたりする。
cue: A doctor asks whether your back hurts all the time.
reply: The pain seems to come and go during the day.
replyJapanese: 痛みは、日中に出たり引いたりするようです。
transferCue: Explain why you do not follow trends in clothes.
transferReply: Fashions come and go, so I buy what I like.
transferReplyJapanese: 流行は移り変わるものなので、自分の好きなものを買います。
nuance: Both verbs change form together: comes and goes, came and went. The order is fixed, so do not say go and come.
nuanceJapanese: 2つの動詞は一緒に変化する: comes and goes, came and went。語順は固定で、go and come とは言わない。

meaning: Be something that you did not expect.
japanese: 驚きである。思いがけないことである。
cue: Your manager has announced that she is leaving.
reply: Her decision to leave came as a surprise to everyone.
replyJapanese: 彼女が辞めるという決断は、みんなにとって驚きでした。
transferCue: Say that you expected your rent to go up.
transferReply: The rent increase didn't come as a surprise to me.
transferReplyJapanese: 家賃の値上げは、私には意外ではありませんでした。
nuance: The surprised person follows to. Often negative: it came as no surprise. Shock and relief fit the same pattern: come as a shock.
nuanceJapanese: 驚く人は to のあとに置く。it came as no surprise のように否定でもよく使う。shock や relief も同じ型で、come as a shock と言える。

meaning: Almost do something.
japanese: もう少しで〜しそうになる。あと一歩まで行く。
cue: Tell a friend about your stressful trip to the airport.
reply: We came close to missing our flight this morning.
replyJapanese: 今朝は、もう少しで飛行機に乗り遅れるところでした。
transferCue: Comfort a friend who finished second in a competition.
transferReply: You didn't win this time, but you came close.
transferReplyJapanese: 今回は勝てなかったけど、あと一歩だったよ。
nuance: After to, use a noun or an -ing form, not an infinitive: come close to winning. Without to, it means almost succeed.
nuanceJapanese: to のあとは名詞か -ing 形で、不定詞にはしない: come close to winning。to なしでは「あと一歩だった」の意味になる。

meaning: Be easy for someone to do without much effort or learning.
japanese: 自然にできる。苦労せずにこなせる。
cue: A friend admires the dinner you made.
reply: Cooking doesn't come naturally to me, so I follow recipes.
replyJapanese: 料理は自然にできるわけではないので、レシピどおりに作っています。
transferCue: Describe a colleague who is good with new customers.
transferReply: Talking to strangers comes naturally to her.
transferReplyJapanese: 彼女は、知らない人とも自然に話せます。
nuance: The skill is the subject and the person follows to: languages come naturally to her. Do not make the person the subject.
nuanceJapanese: 技能が主語で、人は to のあとに置く: languages come naturally to her。人を主語にはしない。

meaning: Finish.
japanese: 終わる。終わりを迎える。
cue: It is the last evening of your holiday.
reply: Our holiday is coming to an end far too quickly.
replyJapanese: 休暇が、あっという間に終わろうとしています。
transferCue: Say when your last job finished.
transferReply: My contract came to an end in March.
transferReplyJapanese: 私の契約は、3月に終了しました。
nuance: A little more formal than end or finish, and used for things that last some time. The thing that finishes is the subject; bring something to an end takes an object.
nuanceJapanese: end や finish より少し改まった言い方で、ある程度続くものに使う。終わるものが主語になる。目的語を取るのは bring something to an end。

meaning: Used when you suddenly remember or realise something.
japanese: そういえば。考えてみると。
cue: A friend asks if you have seen your neighbour lately.
reply: Come to think of it, I haven't seen him all week.
replyJapanese: そういえば、今週は一度も見かけていないな。
transferCue: You are planning a dinner and remember something about a guest.
transferReply: Come to think of it, Ken doesn't eat fish.
transferReplyJapanese: 考えてみたら、ケンは魚を食べないんだった。
nuance: Spoken and informal. It usually opens the sentence, followed by a comma. Come never changes form here.
nuanceJapanese: くだけた話し言葉。ふつう文頭に置き、コンマを続ける。come の形は変えない。

meaning: Again and again, every day for a long time.
japanese: 来る日も来る日も。毎日毎日。
cue: Explain why you left your last job.
reply: I was doing the same tasks day after day.
replyJapanese: 来る日も来る日も、同じ作業をしていました。
transferCue: Describe a disappointing week at the seaside.
transferReply: It rained day after day, so we stayed indoors.
transferReplyJapanese: 毎日毎日雨が降ったので、室内で過ごしました。
nuance: It suggests that something is repeated so often that it becomes boring or tiring. Both nouns stay singular: not days after days.
nuanceJapanese: 何度も繰り返されて、退屈だったり疲れたりする含みがある。名詞は単数のままで、days after days とは言わない。

meaning: Slowly, a little more each day.
japanese: 日ごとに。日に日に。
cue: A friend asks how your father is after his operation.
reply: He's getting stronger day by day.
replyJapanese: 日に日に元気になっています。
transferCue: Describe your garden at the start of spring.
transferReply: Day by day, the garden turned green again.
transferReplyJapanese: 日ごとに、庭に緑が戻ってきました。
nuance: Day by day shows slow change, while day after day shows tiring repetition. It often follows a comparative such as stronger or worse.
nuanceJapanese: day by day は少しずつの変化、day after day はうんざりする繰り返しを表す。stronger や worse などの比較級のあとによく置く。

meaning: Do something well.
japanese: うまくやる。いい仕事をする。
cue: Praise a new team member for her first report.
reply: You did a good job on the customer report.
replyJapanese: 顧客レポート、よくできていましたよ。
transferCue: Recommend a garage to a neighbour.
transferReply: That garage does a good job and never overcharges.
transferReplyJapanese: あの修理工場は仕事が丁寧で、高く請求することもありません。
frame: Do a good job on something
nuance: The verb is do. Other adjectives fit the pattern: do a great job, do a bad job. Good job! on its own is quick praise, especially in American English.
nuanceJapanese: 動詞は do を使う。do a great job, do a bad job のように形容詞を入れ替えられる。Good job! だけで短い褒め言葉になり、特にアメリカ英語で多い。

meaning: Cause damage or have a bad effect.
japanese: 害を与える。悪い影響を及ぼす。
cue: A friend wonders whether to ask a shop for a discount.
reply: Asking for a discount won't do any harm.
replyJapanese: 値引きを頼んでみても、損はありませんよ。
transferCue: Warn a colleague who never leaves his desk.
transferReply: Sitting all day can do harm to your back.
transferReplyJapanese: 一日中座っていると、腰に悪い影響が出ることがあります。
frame: Do harm to something / do someone harm
nuance: The verb is do, not make, and harm is uncountable: not do a harm. It won't do any harm is a common way to suggest trying something.
nuanceJapanese: 動詞は make ではなく do。harm は不可算で、do a harm とは言わない。It won't do any harm は「やってみて損はない」と勧める決まり文句。

meaning: Make someone feel better or healthier.
japanese: 〜のためになる。体や気分によい。
cue: A friend has worked for weeks without a break.
reply: A few days by the sea would do you good.
replyJapanese: 海辺で何日か過ごしたら、きっと元気になるよ。
transferCue: Say how you feel after an evening walk.
transferReply: That walk did me good after sitting all day.
transferReplyJapanese: 一日中座っていたので、あの散歩はいい気分転換になりました。
nuance: The person goes between do and good with no preposition: it will do you good, not do good to you. Common as friendly advice with will or would.
nuanceJapanese: 人は do と good のあいだに前置詞なしで置く: it will do you good。do good to you とは言わない。will や would を使った親しい助言に多い。

meaning: Become ill.
japanese: 病気になる。体調を崩す。
cue: Explain why your family came home early from a trip.
reply: My father fell ill on the second day of the trip.
replyJapanese: 旅行の2日目に、父が体調を崩しました。
transferCue: Ask about travel insurance before a long stay overseas.
transferReply: What happens if I fall ill while I'm abroad?
transferReplyJapanese: 海外にいるあいだに病気になったら、どうなりますか。
nuance: A little formal and mainly British. In everyday speech people say get ill, and American English prefers get sick.
nuanceJapanese: やや改まった言い方で、主にイギリス英語。日常会話では get ill、アメリカ英語では get sick が好まれる。

meaning: Stop talking or making noise.
japanese: 黙り込む。静まり返る。
cue: Describe the moment the head teacher came into a noisy room.
reply: The whole class fell silent when she walked in.
replyJapanese: 彼女が入ってくると、クラス全体が静まり返りました。
transferCue: Describe how a friend reacted to bad news on the phone.
transferReply: He fell silent for a moment, then asked what had happened.
transferReplyJapanese: 彼は一瞬黙り込み、それから何があったのか尋ねました。
nuance: More common in stories and descriptions than in conversation. It describes the change to quiet; stay silent describes the state.
nuanceJapanese: 会話より、物語や描写で多く使う。静かになる変化を表し、その状態が続くことは stay silent で表す。

meaning: Feel sad because you are not included in something.
japanese: 仲間外れにされたと感じる。取り残された気がする。
cue: Explain why you always invite the new student to eat with you.
reply: I don't want her to feel left out at lunch.
replyJapanese: お昼のときに、彼女に仲間外れだと感じてほしくないんです。
transferCue: Everyone at a party discussed a film you had not seen.
transferReply: I felt left out because I hadn't seen the film.
transferReplyJapanese: その映画を見ていなかったので、取り残された気分でした。
nuance: Left is a past participle and never changes: I feel left out, she felt left out. Add of for the activity: left out of the conversation.
nuanceJapanese: left は過去分詞で形は変わらない: I feel left out, she felt left out。活動を示すときは of を付けて left out of the conversation と言う。

meaning: As something different from what usually happens.
japanese: 気分転換に。たまには。
cue: You and your partner always cook at home on Fridays.
reply: Let's eat out tonight for a change.
replyJapanese: たまには、今夜は外で食べよう。
transferCue: Your morning train is usually late.
transferReply: The train arrived on time for a change.
transferReplyJapanese: 珍しく、電車が時間どおりに着きました。
nuance: Usually at the end of the sentence. It can also be a light complaint about what normally happens: you're early for a change.
nuanceJapanese: ふつう文末に置く。you're early for a change のように、いつもの状況への軽い皮肉にもなる。

meaning: Without any doubt.
japanese: 確かに。はっきりと。
cue: A friend asks when your new job starts.
reply: I don't know for certain, but probably in May.
replyJapanese: はっきりとは分かりませんが、たぶん5月です。
transferCue: A colleague asks whether a client will attend a meeting.
transferReply: We can't say for certain that she'll come on Thursday.
transferReplyJapanese: 彼女が木曜日に来るかどうか、確かなことは言えません。
nuance: Mostly after know, say or tell, and often in negative sentences. For sure means the same and is more informal.
nuanceJapanese: know, say, tell のあとに置くことが多く、否定文でよく使う。for sure は同じ意味で、よりくだけた言い方。

meaning: With no result or purpose.
japanese: 無駄に。むなしく。
cue: You hurried to the station, but the train was cancelled.
reply: We ran all the way to the station for nothing.
replyJapanese: 駅までずっと走ったのに、無駄になりました。
transferCue: A meeting was called off after you had prepared for it.
transferReply: I spent the whole weekend preparing those slides for nothing.
transferReplyJapanese: 週末をまるごと使ってあのスライドを準備したのに、無駄でした。
nuance: It comes at the end of the clause. For nothing can also mean free, without paying, so the situation has to make the meaning clear.
nuanceJapanese: 節の終わりに置く。「無料で」の意味にもなるので、どちらの意味かは場面で判断する。

meaning: From now until some later time, when things may change.
japanese: 今のところは。とりあえず。
cue: A friend helping you move asks where the boxes should go.
reply: Just leave them by the door for now.
replyJapanese: とりあえず、ドアのそばに置いておいて。
transferCue: Explain where you are living while you look for a flat.
transferReply: I'm sleeping on my sister's sofa for now.
transferReplyJapanese: 今のところは、姉の家のソファで寝ています。
nuance: It suggests the arrangement is temporary and may change later. For the time being means the same and is a little more formal.
nuanceJapanese: 一時的な取り決めで、あとで変わるかもしれないという含みがある。for the time being は同じ意味で、少し改まった言い方。

meaning: Real and serious, not pretended or only a practice.
japanese: 本物の。本番で。
cue: Your band has rehearsed for weeks, and the concert is tomorrow.
reply: We've practised for weeks, but tomorrow it's for real.
replyJapanese: 何週間も練習してきましたが、明日は本番です。
transferCue: You received an unexpected job offer by email.
transferReply: I thought it was a joke, but the offer was for real.
transferReplyJapanese: 冗談かと思いましたが、そのオファーは本物でした。
nuance: Informal. Are you for real? shows surprise or doubt about what someone has said. In formal writing, use real or genuine.
nuanceJapanese: くだけた表現。Are you for real? は相手の発言への驚きや疑いを表す。改まった文章では real や genuine を使う。

meaning: As a shorter form of a name.
japanese: 略して。短くして。
cue: Introduce yourself to your new classmates.
reply: My name is Alexandra, but everyone calls me Alex for short.
replyJapanese: アレクサンドラといいますが、みんなは短くアレックスと呼びます。
transferCue: Explain a name that a new colleague will hear at work.
transferReply: This is the information technology team, or IT for short.
transferReplyJapanese: こちらは情報技術チーム、略してITチームです。
nuance: It follows the short form, usually at the end of the sentence. Short for works the other way round: Alex is short for Alexandra.
nuanceJapanese: 短い形のあと、ふつう文末に置く。short for は向きが逆で、Alex is short for Alexandra のように使う。

meaning: Good in the end, even if it seems bad now.
japanese: 結局はそれでよい。かえってよい結果になる。
cue: A friend did not get a job that had very long hours.
reply: Maybe it's for the best, given those long hours.
replyJapanese: あの長時間勤務を考えると、かえってよかったのかもしれないよ。
transferCue: Look back on a house move that you did not want.
transferReply: I hated moving, but it turned out for the best.
transferReplyJapanese: 引っ越しは嫌でしたが、結果的にはそれでよかったです。
frame: Be for the best / turn out for the best
nuance: Used to comfort someone or to accept a disappointment, often after maybe or probably. Do your best is different: it means try as hard as you can.
nuanceJapanese: 相手を慰めたり、残念な結果を受け入れたりするときに使い、maybe や probably のあとに多い。do your best は「全力を尽くす」で別の表現。

meaning: Over the whole of your body.
japanese: 頭のてっぺんからつま先まで。全身。
cue: Your children come in from the garden after heavy rain.
reply: The kids were covered in mud from head to toe.
replyJapanese: 子どもたちは、全身泥だらけでした。
transferCue: Describe what a guest wore to a wedding.
transferReply: She was dressed in green from head to toe.
transferReplyJapanese: 彼女は頭のてっぺんからつま先まで、緑ずくめでした。
frame: Be covered / dressed in something from head to toe
nuance: No articles: from head to toe, not from the head to the toe. It often follows covered, dressed or soaked. From head to foot means the same.
nuanceJapanese: 冠詞なしで from head to toe。from the head to the toe とは言わない。covered, dressed, soaked のあとによく置く。from head to foot も同じ意味。

meaning: From the beginning to the end of something.
japanese: 最初から最後まで。
cue: A friend asks what you thought of a long film.
reply: I enjoyed that film from start to finish.
replyJapanese: あの映画は、最初から最後まで楽しめました。
transferCue: Praise the colleague who organised the office move.
transferReply: She managed the whole office move from start to finish.
transferReplyJapanese: 彼女はオフィスの引っ越しを、最初から最後まで取り仕切りました。
frame: Do something from start to finish
nuance: No articles: not from the start to the finish. It stresses that nothing was left out. From beginning to end means the same.
nuanceJapanese: 冠詞なしで使い、from the start to the finish とは言わない。途中を一切省かないことを強調する。from beginning to end も同じ意味。

meaning: Starting at that time and continuing after it.
japanese: それ以来。そのときからずっと。
cue: Explain why you always back up your work.
reply: I lost an essay once and saved everything twice from then on.
replyJapanese: 一度レポートを失くしてしまい、それ以来すべて二重に保存するようにしました。
transferCue: Tell how you and a colleague became friends after a difficult project.
transferReply: From then on, we had lunch together every Friday.
transferReplyJapanese: それ以来、私たちは毎週金曜日に一緒に昼食をとるようになりました。
nuance: Used with past tenses for a point in the past. For a change that starts at the present moment, say from now on.
nuanceJapanese: 過去のある時点について、過去時制とともに使う。今この時点から始まる変化には from now on を使う。

meaning: Manage to contact someone, especially by phone.
japanese: 連絡を取る。連絡がつく。
cue: A client has not answered any of your calls today.
reply: I've been trying to get hold of her all morning.
replyJapanese: 午前中ずっと、彼女に連絡を取ろうとしています。
transferCue: Tell a friend how to reach you while you are travelling.
transferReply: You can get hold of me on this number after six.
transferReplyJapanese: 6時以降なら、この番号で私に連絡がつきます。
nuance: British English has no article; American English often says get a hold of. With a thing as the object it means obtain: get hold of a ticket.
nuanceJapanese: イギリス英語では冠詞なし、アメリカ英語では get a hold of も多い。物を目的語にすると「手に入れる」の意味になる: get hold of a ticket。

meaning: Be told to leave your job.
japanese: 首になる。解雇される。
cue: Explain why a colleague no longer works at your company.
reply: He got the sack for being late every day.
replyJapanese: 彼は毎日遅刻して、首になりました。
transferCue: A friend keeps taking long personal calls at work.
transferReply: You'll get the sack if your boss finds out.
transferReplyJapanese: 上司に知られたら、首になるよ。
nuance: Informal and mainly British; American English says get fired. Give someone the sack and the verb sack describe the employer's side.
nuanceJapanese: くだけた言い方で、主にイギリス英語。アメリカ英語では get fired。雇う側の動作は give someone the sack や動詞 sack で表す。

meaning: Say the most important thing without wasting time.
japanese: 要点を言う。本題に入る。
cue: A meeting is almost out of time when you start to speak.
reply: We only have five minutes, so I'll get to the point.
replyJapanese: 5分しかないので、本題に入ります。
transferCue: Complain about a long speech at a conference.
transferReply: He talked for an hour and never got to the point.
transferReplyJapanese: 彼は1時間話しましたが、最後まで要点に触れませんでした。
nuance: Said to another person, it sounds impatient, so it is safer about yourself. Get straight to the point adds emphasis.
nuanceJapanese: 相手に向けて言うといらだって聞こえるので、自分について使うのが無難。get straight to the point で強調できる。

meaning: Become more ill or more serious.
japanese: 悪化する。ひどくなる。
cue: You are deciding whether your cold needs a doctor.
reply: If my cough gets worse, I'll see a doctor.
replyJapanese: 咳がひどくなったら、医者に行きます。
transferCue: Tell a physiotherapist about an old running injury.
transferReply: My knee has been getting worse since the race.
transferReplyJapanese: レース以来、膝の状態が悪くなってきています。
nuance: Worse is the comparative of bad: never get more bad or get worser. Get better is the opposite. It is also used for weather, traffic and other situations.
nuanceJapanese: worse は bad の比較級。get more bad や get worser とは言わない。反対は get better。天気や渋滞など、状況全般にも使う。

meaning: Make people let you do what you want.
japanese: 自分の思いどおりにする。我を通す。
cue: Describe the youngest child in your family.
reply: My little brother always gets his own way.
replyJapanese: 弟は、いつも自分の思いどおりにします。
transferCue: Tell how a determined colleague changed the holiday rota.
transferReply: She kept arguing until she got her own way.
transferReplyJapanese: 彼女は、自分の希望が通るまで言い張りました。
nuance: Your changes with the person: get his own way, get her own way. It is a little critical, suggesting the person ignores what others want. American English often says get your way.
nuanceJapanese: your は人に合わせて変える: get his own way, get her own way。他人の希望を顧みないという、やや批判的な響きがある。アメリカ英語では get your way も多い。

meaning: Have a baby.
japanese: 出産する。子を産む。
cue: Share happy family news with a colleague.
reply: My sister gave birth to a baby girl last night.
replyJapanese: 昨夜、姉が女の子を出産しました。
transferCue: Explain why your cat needs a quiet room this week.
transferReply: Our cat is about to give birth to her kittens.
transferReplyJapanese: うちの猫は、もうすぐ子猫を産みます。
nuance: No article before birth, and the baby follows to. The mother is the subject; for the child, say be born.
nuanceJapanese: birth に冠詞は付かず、生まれる子は to のあとに置く。主語は母親で、子どもの側からは be born と言う。

meaning: Promise seriously to do something.
japanese: 約束する。誓う。
cue: You are invited out on the day you promised to help a friend.
reply: I gave my word that I'd help Dan move on Saturday.
replyJapanese: 土曜日はダンの引っ越しを手伝うと約束したんです。
transferCue: Explain why you trust a friend with a secret.
transferReply: She gave her word that she wouldn't tell anyone.
transferReplyJapanese: 彼女は、誰にも言わないと約束してくれました。
nuance: Your changes with the person: I gave my word, she gave her word. Word stays singular. It is more serious than promise; keep your word means do what you promised.
nuanceJapanese: your は人に合わせて変える: I gave my word, she gave her word。word は単数のまま。promise より重い言い方で、keep your word は「約束を守る」。

meaning: Become too old to eat or drink safely.
japanese: 腐る。傷む。
cue: You smell the milk before pouring it into your tea.
reply: I think this milk has gone bad.
replyJapanese: この牛乳、傷んでいると思います。
transferCue: Your flatmate has left cooked chicken on the table.
transferReply: Put the chicken in the fridge before it goes bad.
transferReplyJapanese: 傷む前に、鶏肉を冷蔵庫に入れておいて。
nuance: Used for food and drink. British English often says go off with the same meaning. Went and gone are the past forms.
nuanceJapanese: 食べ物や飲み物に使う。イギリス英語では同じ意味で go off もよく使う。過去形は went、過去分詞は gone。

meaning: Become unable to pay your debts.
japanese: 破産する。倒産する。
cue: Explain why a shop in your street has closed.
reply: The bookshop went bankrupt after its rent doubled.
replyJapanese: 家賃が2倍になり、その書店は倒産しました。
transferCue: Warn your business partner about falling sales.
transferReply: We could go bankrupt if sales don't improve soon.
transferReplyJapanese: 売上がすぐに改善しなければ、倒産するおそれがあります。
nuance: Bankrupt is an adjective, so there is no article. It is used for both people and companies. Go bust is an informal equivalent.
nuanceJapanese: bankrupt は形容詞なので冠詞は付かない。個人にも会社にも使う。go bust はくだけた同義表現。

meaning: Suddenly be unable to remember something that you know.
japanese: 頭が真っ白になる。ど忘れする。
cue: Describe the worst moment of a job interview.
reply: My mind went blank when they asked about my last job.
replyJapanese: 前の仕事について聞かれたとき、頭が真っ白になりました。
transferCue: Explain why exams are hard for you.
transferReply: I always go blank when I see an exam paper.
transferReplyJapanese: 試験用紙を見ると、いつも頭が真っ白になります。
nuance: The subject is usually my mind, though a person can also go blank. It is temporary: the memory comes back later. A screen can go blank too.
nuanceJapanese: 主語はふつう my mind だが、人を主語にもできる。一時的なもので、あとで思い出せる。画面が消えるときにも go blank を使う。
